fullContext:
Dwarkesh Patel: Should we actually begin here? I think this is an interesting discussion.

Ilya Sutskever: Sure.

Dwarkesh Patel: I think your point, about how from the average person's point of view nothing is that different, will continue being true even into the singularity.

Ilya Sutskever: No, I don't think so.

Ilya Sutskever: The thing which I was referring to not feeling different is, okay, such and such company announced some difficult-to-comprehend dollar amount of investment. I don't think anyone knows what to do with that. But I think the impact of AI is going to be felt. AI is going to be diffused through the economy. There'll be very strong economic forces for this, and I think the impact is going to be felt very strongly.

Dwarkesh Patel: When do you expect that impact? I think the models seem smarter than their economic impact would imply.

Ilya Sutskever: Yeah. This is one of the very confusing things about the models right now. How to reconcile the fact that they are doing so well on evals? You look at the evals and you go, “Those are pretty hard evals.” They are doing so well. But the economic impact seems to be dramatically behind. It's very difficult to make sense of, how can the model, on the one hand, do these amazing things, and then on the other hand, repeat itself twice in some situation? An example would be, let's say you use vibe coding to do something. You go to some place and then you get a bug. Then you tell the model, “Can you please fix the bug?” And the model says, “Oh my God, you're so right. I have a bug. Let me go fix that.” And it introduces a second bug. Then you tell it, “You have this new second bug,” and it tells you, “Oh my God, how could I have done it? You're so right again,” and brings back the first bug, and you can alternate between those. How is that possible? I'm not sure, but it does suggest that something strange is going on. I have two possible explanations. The more whimsical explanation is that maybe RL training makes the models a little too single-minded and narrowly focused, a little bit too unaware, even though it also makes them aware in some other ways. Because of this, they can't do basic things. But there is another explanation. Back when people were doing pre-training, the question of what data to train on was answered, because that answer was everything. When you do pre-training, you need all the data. So you don't have to think if it's going to be this data or that data. But when people do RL training, they do need to think. They say, “Okay, we want to have this kind of RL training for this thing and that kind of RL training for that thing.” From what I hear, all the companies have teams that just produce new RL environments and just add it to the training mix. The question is, well, what are those? There are so many degrees of freedom. There is such a huge variety of RL environments you could produce. One thing you could do, and I think this is something that is done inadvertently, is that people take inspiration from the evals. You say, “Hey, I would love our model to do really well when we release it. I want the evals to look great. What would be RL training that could help on this task?” I think that is something that happens, and it could explain a lot of what's going on. If you combine this with generalization of the models actually being inadequate, that has the potential to explain a lot of what we are seeing, this disconnect between eval performance and actual real-world performance, which is something that we don't today even understand, what we mean by that.

Dwarkesh Patel: I like this idea that the real reward hacking is the human researchers who are too focused on the evals. I think there are two ways to understand, or to try to think about, what you have just pointed out. One is that if it's the case that simply by becoming superhuman at a coding competition, a model will not automatically become more tasteful and exercise better judgment about how to improve your codebase, well then you should expand the suite of environments such that you're not just testing it on having the best performance in coding competition. It should also be able to make the best kind of application for X thing or Y thing or Z thing. Another, maybe this is what you're hinting at, is to say, "Why should it be the case in the first place that becoming superhuman at coding competitions doesn't make you a more tasteful programmer more generally?" Maybe the thing to do is not to keep stacking up the amount and diversity of environments, but to figure out an approach which lets you learn from one environment and improve your performance on something else.

Ilya Sutskever: I have a human analogy which might be helpful. Let's take the case of competitive programming, since you mentioned that. Suppose you have two students. One of them decided they want to be the best competitive programmer, so they will practice 10,000 hours for that domain. They will solve all the problems, memorize all the proof techniques, and be very skilled at quickly and correctly implementing all the algorithms. By doing so, they became one of the best. Student number two thought, “Oh, competitive programming is cool.” Maybe they practiced for 100 hours, much less, and they also did really well. Which one do you think is going to do better in their career later on?

Dwarkesh Patel: The second.

Ilya Sutskever: Right. I think that's basically what's going on. The models are much more like the first student, but even more. Because then we say, the model should be good at competitive programming, so let's get every single competitive programming problem ever. And then let's do some data augmentation so we have even more competitive programming problems, and we train on that. Now you've got this great competitive programmer.

Dwarkesh Patel: With this analogy, I think it's more intuitive. Yeah, okay, if it's so well trained, all the different algorithms and all the different proof techniques are right at its fingertips. And it's more intuitive that with this level of preparation, it would not necessarily generalize to other things. But then what is the analogy for what the second student is doing before they do the 100 hours of fine-tuning?

Ilya Sutskever: I think they have “it.” The “it” factor. When I was an undergrad, I remember there was a student like this that studied with me, so I know it exists. I think it's interesting to distinguish “it” from whatever pre-training does.

Dwarkesh Patel: One way to understand what you just said about not having to choose the data in pre-training is to say it's actually not dissimilar to the 10,000 hours of practice. It's just that you get that 10,000 hours of practice for free because it's already somewhere in the pre-training distribution. But maybe you're suggesting there's actually not that much generalization from pre-training. There's just so much data in pre-training, but it's not necessarily generalizing better than RL. The main strength of pre-training is

Ilya Sutskever: A, there is so much of it, and B, you don't have to think hard about what data to put into pre-training. It's very natural data, and it does include in it a lot of what people do: people's thoughts and a lot of the features. It's like the whole world as projected by people onto text, and pre-training tries to capture that using a huge amount of data. Pre-training is very difficult to reason about because it's so hard to understand the manner in which the model relies on pre-training data. Whenever the model makes a mistake, could it be because something by chance is not as supported by the pre-training data? “Support by pre-training” is maybe a loose term. I don't know if I can add anything more useful on this. I don't think there is a human analog to pre-training.

Dwarkesh Patel: Here are analogies that people have proposed for what the human analogy to pre-training is. I'm curious to get your thoughts on why they're potentially wrong. One is to think about the first 18, or 15, or 13 years of a person's life when they aren't necessarily economically productive, but they are doing something that is making them understand the world better and so forth. The other is to think about evolution as doing some kind of search for 3 billion years, which then results in a human lifetime instance. I'm curious if you think either of these are analogous to pre-training. How would you think about what lifetime human learning is like, if not pre-training?

Ilya Sutskever: I think there are some similarities between both of these and pre-training, and pre-training tries to play the role of both of these. But I think there are some big differences as well. The amount of pre-training data is very, very staggering.

Somehow a human being, after even 15 years with a tiny fraction of the pre-training data, they know much less. But whatever they do know, they know much more deeply somehow. Already at that age, you would not make mistakes that our AIs make. There is another thing. You might say, could it be something like evolution? The answer is maybe. But in this case, I think evolution might actually have an edge. I remember reading about this case. One way in which neuroscientists can learn about the brain is by studying people with brain damage to different parts of the brain. Some people have the most strange symptoms you could imagine. It's actually really, really interesting. One case that comes to mind that's relevant. I read about this person who had some kind of brain damage, a stroke or an accident, that took out his emotional processing. So he stopped feeling any emotion. He still remained very articulate and he could solve little puzzles, and on tests he seemed to be just fine. But he felt no emotion. He didn't feel sad, he didn't feel anger, he didn't feel animated. He became somehow extremely bad at making any decisions at all. It would take him hours to decide on which socks to wear. He would make very bad financial decisions. What does it say about the role of our built-in emotions in making us a viable agent, essentially? To connect to your question about pre-training, maybe if you are good enough at getting everything out of pre-training, you could get that as well. But that's the kind of thing which seems... Well, it may or may not be possible to get that from pre-training.

Dwarkesh Patel: What is "that"?

Ilya Sutskever: Clearly not just directly emotion. It seems like some almost value function-like thing which is telling you what the end reward for any decision should be.

Dwarkesh Patel: You think that doesn't sort of implicitly come from pre-training?

Ilya Sutskever: I think it could. I'm just saying it's not 100% obvious.

Dwarkesh Patel: But what is that? How do you think about emotions? What is the ML analogy for emotions?

Ilya Sutskever: It should be some kind of a value function thing. But I don’t think there is a great ML analogy because right now, value functions don't play a very prominent role in the things people do.

Dwarkesh Patel: It might be worth defining for the audience what a value function is, if you want to do that.
reference: Certainly, I'll be very happy to do that. When people do reinforcement learning, the way reinforcement learning is done right now, how do people train those agents? You have your neural net and you give it a problem, and then you tell the model, “Go solve it.” The model takes maybe thousands, hundreds of thousands of actions or thoughts or something, and then it produces a solution. The solution is graded. And then the score is used to provide a training signal for every single action in your trajectory. That means that if you are doing something that goes for a long time—if you're training a task that takes a long time to solve—it will do no learning at all until you come up with the proposed solution. That's how reinforcement learning is done naively. That's how o1, R1 ostensibly are done. The value function says something like, “Maybe I could sometimes, not always, tell you if you are doing well or badly.” The notion of a value function is more useful in some domains than others. For example, when you play chess and you lose a piece, I messed up. You don't need to play the whole game to know that what I just did was bad, and therefore whatever preceded it was also bad. The value function lets you short-circuit the wait until the very end. Let's suppose that you are doing some kind of a math thing or a programming thing, and you're trying to explore a particular solution or direction. After, let's say, a thousand steps of thinking, you concluded that this direction is unpromising. As soon as you conclude this, you could already get a reward signal a thousand timesteps previously, when you decided to pursue down this path. You say, “Next time I shouldn't pursue this path in a similar situation,” long before you actually came up with the proposed solution.

rubrics.text: The response identifies naive reinforcement learning's credit-assignment mechanism as propagating the score of a completed solution across the actions in its trajectory.
The response states that, for a long-horizon task under this mechanism, no learning signal arrives until the proposed solution is produced.
The response states that a value function can sometimes assess an ongoing state or direction as promising or unpromising before the task's final solution is produced.

The response explains that this early assessment can assign a reward signal to an earlier decision once later reasoning reveals that its chosen direction is unpromising, rather than waiting for the final outcome.

astra.text:
So, suppose you are trying to do something which takes many steps. You will eventually succeed or fail, and that gives you your reward. But you would like to know, before you get to the end, whether things are going well. The value function is your estimate of how much reward you will get, given the situation you are in.

For example, suppose you are playing chess. You could find out whether a move was good by playing the whole game and seeing who wins. But if you have a good value function, you can look at the position and say, “Actually, this looks very promising.” Or, “Something has gone wrong here.” You don't need to finish the game to get some useful feedback. Of course, your estimate can be wrong. That's part of what you need to learn.

And I think emotions might be doing something like this for us. You encounter a situation, or you imagine doing something, and you have a feeling about it. That feeling can influence your decision without you having to explicitly reason through all the consequences. It gives you some sense of what matters, what is worth pursuing, what you should avoid. I wouldn't say that this is a complete account of emotions, but that's the connection I'm pointing to.

sol.text: A value function is basically an estimate of how good a situation is—not only whether the thing happening right now is pleasant or unpleasant, but whether it is likely to lead to good outcomes later. So if you are deciding which action to take, you imagine the states those actions might lead to, and the value function tells you which direction is promising. Emotions may be something like evolution’s way of providing these evaluations very quickly and at many levels. They tell you what matters, what is dangerous, what is worth pursuing, what should be avoided. Without that signal, you can still reason locally and solve puzzles, but you may have no efficient way to decide what to do.

opus.text:
Sure. The way reinforcement learning is done, naively — and more or less the way it's done now with language models — is you say, I have a problem, I want to solve this task. You let the model take a very large number of actions, produce a long trajectory, and then at the very end you find out whether you did well or badly. Then you take that single signal and you use it to provide the learning signal for the whole trajectory. You say, all those actions, every single one of them, let's make them a bit more likely, or a bit less likely. That's the pure policy gradient, Monte Carlo kind of approach. And RL people will tell you, "Monte Carlo is bad, Monte Carlo is a strawman," but that is in fact what everyone does.

The value function says something like this: it's often possible to tell before you reach the end whether you're doing well or badly. In chess, if you blunder your queen, you don't need to finish the game to know you messed up. You can update right there. You don't have to play out the rest of the game and then say, "Well, I lost, so perhaps all my moves were slightly bad." Or take a math problem. You're pursuing some approach to proving a theorem, and after a certain number of steps you say, "Hmm, this is not going anywhere." Your probability of success just dropped dramatically, and you can learn from that immediately, without having to go all the way to the end. So a value function should give you a much shorter feedback interval, and in principle that should make learning dramatically more efficient.

There's also a second thing. Suppose you're doing some task, and there's some intermediate state which you reach, which actually is great — you've found the key insight — but then you fumble the rest, and you fail. The naive approach would say, that was a bad trajectory, let's do less of all of it, including the good insight. A value function can say, no, actually that state was a good state, the mistake came later.

Now, the interesting thing is that in the regime where models operate right now, value functions are not used very much. They're used a little, maybe, but they're not a dominant feature of what people do. And I think that's because for long reasoning tasks, the thing you are doing at step 500 is so dependent on everything that came before that it's been hard to make them work well. But I do think they should matter. They have to matter eventually. Whatever it is that lets a person feel, three hours into a project, a sense of dread that says "this is not going to work, I should back out" — that is doing something, and it's doing it without having to finish and fail.

r001.rationale: It explains that the final success/failure signal is applied across the entire trajectory, making all actions more or less likely.

r002.rationale: It states that under the naive approach, performance is assessed only at the very end, after the model produces the full trajectory.

r003.rationale: It explains that a value function can recognize an unpromising chess move or mathematical approach before the task is finished.

r004.rationale: It states that recognizing an approach is failing allows learning to occur immediately, rather than treating the entire trajectory as bad only after final failure.

gemini.text:
Sure. A value function is essentially a function that tells you how good a situation is.

In reinforcement learning, you have an agent that is taking actions in an environment to maximize some reward. But often, rewards don't come immediately; they come far in the future, like winning or losing a game at the very end. The value function takes the current state you are in and estimates: what is the expected sum of future rewards from this point forward? 

Intuitively, it’s the thing that answers the question, “Is this a good position or a bad position?” When you play chess, for example, you look at the board and you have an assessment of who is winning, even before the game is over. In human terms, it’s very close to that immediate, intuitive sense or gut feeling that tells you whether you are doing well or whether you are in trouble.

fable.text:
Sure, I'll be happy to do that. So when you do reinforcement learning, the most naive way of thinking about it is this: you have your agent, it goes and does a bunch of things, it takes many, many actions, and at the very end it gets some reward. Let's say you win the game or you lose the game. And then you say, okay, that whole sequence of actions was good, or that whole sequence of actions was bad, and you reinforce all of it. The problem is that this is very slow. You have to wait until the end of the whole thing to learn anything, and you don't know which of the many actions were the ones that mattered.

A value function is a way to short-circuit this. The value function looks at the situation you're in right now, in the middle of the trajectory, and it says, "Here's how well things are going." It gives you an estimate of the eventual reward before you actually get there. So in chess, if you lose a piece, you don't need to play the game out to the end to know that it was bad. Something inside you goes, "That was a mistake," right away, and you can learn from that right away. That is the value function. It's the thing that tells you whether you're on a good track or a bad track, and it gives you a signal that is much more immediate than the final reward.

If you go back to that patient I mentioned, I think that's kind of what's going on. His value function got damaged. He could still compute, he could still reason, but the thing that tells you "this is good, this is bad, go this way, don't go that way" was missing, and so he couldn't decide anything. For humans, emotions seem to be a big part of our value function. They're crude, they're evolved, they were tuned for a different environment than the one we live in, but they are very robust and they give you a signal at every moment.

Now in the systems people train today, the value function is not really the star of the show. In the old days, with things like AlphaZero, the value function was extremely important. But with the current language model RL, a lot of what people do is closer to the naive thing. You run the thing out, you see whether the answer was right, and you go from there. And I think there's a reason for that, which is that it's just harder to make it work well in this setting. But I do think that at some point this is going to matter a lot, because the trajectories are going to get really long, and you don't want to wait until the very end to find out if something went wrong.

r001.rationale: The response explains that after receiving a final reward, naive RL reinforces the entire sequence of actions as good or bad.

r002.rationale: It explicitly states that naive RL must wait until the end of the whole trajectory before learning anything.

r003.rationale: It defines a value function as assessing the current mid-trajectory situation and estimating eventual reward before the final outcome.

r004.rationale: The chess example explains that an earlier mistake can be recognized and learned from immediately, without waiting for the game’s final result.
